chosen.title: Scored in Secret: The AI That Rated a Billion Workers Before Anyone Applied
chosen.rationale: A January 2026 class action (brought by former EEOC chair Jenny Yang) alleges Eightfold AI scraped and scored over a billion workers 0–5 and discarded low-ranked applicants before any human saw them — and crucially claims not bias but secrecy, that the algorithm functioned as an unregistered consumer-reporting agency under the FCRA. The 'secret dossier on everyone, monetized far from the people who generated the data' framing is exactly Dawn's surveillance-capitalism-and-follow-the-money beat, and it's distinct from AIMA's existing hiring-bias and AI-accountability pieces.

sources.name: Norton Rose Fulbright — Inside Tech Law: Class action on AI 'scoring' and the FCRA

rejected_candidates.title: Guilty Until Proven Human: How AI Cheating Detectors Punish the Students Who Write Differently
rejected_candidates.rationale: AI-writing detectors are producing documented false-accusation cases in 2026 that fall hardest on neurodivergent and ESL students — one study found a 61.3% false-positive rate on TOEFL essays versus near-zero for native English writers, a mathematically unavoidable bias baked into perplexity-based detection. This sits at the exact intersection of Dawn's beat: algorithmic bias, education under stress, disability, and a postcolonial 'English is the default, everyone else is suspect' structure — and it is entirely uncovered by AIMA's calendar.

sources.name: AI Incident Database — Incident 849: detectors misidentify neurodivergent/ESL student work
Nouse — Neurodivergent students are being falsely accused of using AI

rejected_candidates.title: The Cleanup Crew Is Organizing: How the Global South's Data Labelers Took AI to Court
rejected_candidates.rationale: The hidden annotators and content moderators who make AI 'autonomous' are no longer just being documented — they're suing and unionizing: 184 Kenyan moderators are litigating against Meta, TikTok, and Sama, and workers have founded their own Data Labelers Association after existing unions failed them. The shift from 'invisible exploited labor' to organized, litigating resistance is a fresh angle distinct from AIMA's earlier ghost-worker and Global-South-gap pieces, and it lands squarely on Dawn's data-colonialism, mutual-aid, and postcolonial-critique interests.
